topics.name: Genetic Disorders
topics.teaser: When the code or the chromosome count goes wrong.

questions.text: A pure-breeding tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure-breeding dwarf pea plant (tt). What will be the phenotype of all F1 offspring?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Determine the gametes**
A TT plant produces only T gametes and a tt plant produces only t gametes, since each parent is homozygous and contributes one allele per gamete.

**Step 2: Form the F1 genotype**
Fusion of a T gamete with a t gamete gives every F1 offspring the genotype Tt, a heterozygote carrying one dominant and one recessive allele.

**Step 3: Apply the law of dominance**
Mendel's law of dominance states that in a heterozygote, only the dominant allele expresses itself in the phenotype while the recessive allele remains hidden. Since T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf), all Tt plants appear tall.

**Final Answer**
Because every F1 plant is heterozygous Tt and tallness is dominant, the entire F1 generation is uniformly tall.
Final answer: A) All tall
questions.tip: Whenever both parents are pure-breeding (homozygous) for contrasting traits, the F1 is always uniform and shows the dominant phenotype.

questions.text: When Mendel self-pollinated the F1 tall plants (Tt), the F2 generation showed which phenotypic ratio?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the cross**
Selfing a heterozygous Tt plant means Tt is crossed with Tt, so each parent can contribute either a T or a t allele to its gametes in equal proportion.

**Step 2: Build the Punnett square**
Combining the gametes T and t from each parent gives four equally likely zygote combinations: TT, Tt, Tt, and tt.

**Step 3: Convert genotypes to phenotypes**
TT and Tt (three out of four) are tall because T is dominant, while only tt (one out of four) is dwarf, since two recessive alleles are needed to express the recessive trait.

**Final Answer**
This 3 tall to 1 dwarf outcome is Mendel's classic monohybrid F2 phenotypic ratio, arising from the law of segregation.
Final answer: C) 3:1
questions.tip: Monohybrid genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 (TT:Tt:tt) but phenotypic ratio is 3:1 because TT and Tt look alike.

questions.text: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that:
options: The two alleles of a gene separate from each other during gamete formation
Two genes on different chromosomes assort independently
A dominant allele always masks a recessive allele completely
Genes on the same chromosome are inherited together
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the physical basis of the law**
Each individual carries two alleles for a given gene, one inherited from each parent, located on homologous chromosomes.

**Step 2: Link this to meiosis**
During meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate at anaphase I, so the two alleles of a gene that were together in the parent cell are segregated into different gametes.

**Step 3: Eliminate distractors**
Independent assortment describes behaviour of genes on different chromosome pairs, complete dominance describes phenotype expression, and linkage describes genes on the same chromosome staying together, none of which define segregation itself.

**Final Answer**
The law of segregation specifically concerns the separation of the two alleles of a single gene into different gametes, ensuring gametes are pure for that gene.
Final answer: A) The two alleles of a gene separate from each other during gamete formation
questions.tip: Law of Segregation = law of purity of gametes; each gamete gets only ONE allele of a gene pair.

questions.text: A test cross is performed by crossing an individual of unknown genotype with:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the purpose of a test cross**
A test cross is used to determine whether an individual showing the dominant phenotype is homozygous dominant or heterozygous.

**Step 2: Understand why a homozygous recessive tester is used**
A homozygous recessive individual contributes only recessive alleles to every gamete, so it cannot mask or add any dominant allele of its own, making it a genetically neutral tester.

**Step 3: Predict outcomes**
If the unknown parent is homozygous dominant (TT), all offspring will show the dominant phenotype; if it is heterozygous (Tt), offspring will show a 1:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes, revealing the unknown genotype.

**Final Answer**
Crossing with a homozygous recessive individual is the standard test cross because it unambiguously reveals the alleles present in the gametes of the unknown parent.
Final answer: B) A homozygous recessive individual
questions.tip: Test cross ratio 1:1 confirms heterozygosity; all-dominant offspring confirm homozygous dominant genotype.

questions.text: In Mendel's dihybrid cross between plants with round, yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled, green seeds (rryy), the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Determine F1 genotype**
Crossing RRYY with rryy gives gametes RY and ry respectively, so every F1 plant is RrYy, heterozygous for both genes.

**Step 2: Apply independent assortment in F1 gametes**
Since the seed shape and seed colour genes assort independently of each other during meiosis, the RrYy plant produces four types of gametes in equal frequency: RY, Ry, rY, and ry.

**Step 3: Build the 4x4 Punnett square**
Combining these gametes from both parents in a Punnett square yields 16 equally likely combinations that fall into four phenotypic classes: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, and wrinkled green.

**Step 4: Count the classes**
Counting the 16 boxes gives 9 round-yellow, 3 round-green, 3 wrinkled-yellow, and 1 wrinkled-green, the classic dihybrid ratio.

**Final Answer**
This 9:3:3:1 ratio demonstrates that the two gene pairs assort independently of each other, confirming the law of independent assortment.
Final answer: C) 9:3:3:1
questions.tip: 9:3:3:1 always comes from selfing a double heterozygote (AaBb x AaBb) when genes are on different chromosome pairs.

questions.text: What is the genotypic ratio obtained when a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is self-pollinated?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: List the gametes**
A Tt plant produces T and t gametes in equal proportion, since the two alleles segregate equally during meiosis.

**Step 2: Combine gametes in a Punnett square**
Selfing Tt x Tt gives four combinations: TT, Tt, Tt, and tt, each equally likely.

**Step 3: Group identical genotypes**
Among the four combinations, one is TT, two are Tt, and one is tt, giving a genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

**Final Answer**
Unlike the phenotypic ratio of 3:1 (since TT and Tt both look tall), the genotypic ratio distinguishes homozygotes from heterozygotes and is 1:2:1.
Final answer: B) 1:2:1
questions.tip: Remember: phenotypic ratio 3:1 but genotypic ratio 1:2:1 for a monohybrid F2 - do not confuse the two.

questions.text: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment applies most accurately to genes that are:
options: Located on the same chromosome close together
Located on the same chromosome far apart
Located on the X chromosome only
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the statement of the law**
The law of independent assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of alleles is independent of the other pair.

**Step 2: Connect to chromosome behaviour**
This independence occurs because genes on different, non-homologous chromosome pairs orient randomly with respect to each other at metaphase I of meiosis, so their alleles are distributed to gametes independently.

**Step 3: Consider the exception**
Genes located on the same chromosome, especially close together, tend to be inherited together (linkage) and do not assort fully independently, which is why Mendel's law holds strictly only for genes on different chromosome pairs.

**Final Answer**
True independent assortment is best observed for genes located on different, non-homologous chromosomes, since their inheritance is not physically linked.
Final answer: C) Located on different (non-homologous) chromosomes
questions.tip: Linkage is the major exception to independent assortment - genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, especially if close.

questions.text: A dihybrid test cross between a double heterozygote (AaBb) and a double recessive (aabb) individual is expected to produce offspring in the ratio:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Determine gametes of each parent**
The AaBb parent, following independent assortment, produces four gamete types in equal frequency: AB, Ab, aB, and ab. The aabb parent produces only ab gametes.

**Step 2: Combine gametes**
Fusing each of the four AaBb gamete types with the single ab gamete type gives four offspring genotypes: AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, and aabb, each in equal proportion.

**Step 3: Relate genotype to phenotype**
Since the tester parent contributes only recessive alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reflects the alleles received from the AaBb parent, so all four phenotypic classes appear with equal frequency.

**Final Answer**
A dihybrid test cross therefore gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio of the four possible phenotype combinations, directly revealing the gamete ratio produced by the heterozygous parent.
Final answer: C) 1:1:1:1
questions.tip: A test cross always reveals the true gamete ratio of the unknown parent because the recessive tester adds no dominant alleles.

questions.text: In a cross between AaBb and aaBb (where A and B are dominant and assort independently), what proportion of the offspring is expected to show the recessive phenotype for both traits (aabb)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Split into two independent monohybrid crosses**
Since the genes assort independently, analyse the A gene and B gene crosses separately: Aa x aa for the first gene, and Bb x Bb for the second gene.

**Step 2: Find probability of aa from Aa x aa**
Aa x aa produces gametes A/a from one parent and only a from the other, giving offspring Aa and aa in a 1:1 ratio, so the probability of aa is 1/2.

**Step 3: Find probability of bb from Bb x Bb**
Bb x Bb is a standard monohybrid self-cross giving BB:Bb:bb in 1:2:1 ratio, so the probability of bb is 1/4.

**Step 4: Apply the product rule**
Because the two gene pairs assort independently, the combined probability of an offspring being aabb is the product of the two individual probabilities: 1/2 multiplied by 1/4.

**Final Answer**
Multiplying 1/2 by 1/4 gives 1/8, so 1/8 of the offspring are expected to be aabb, doubly recessive.
Final answer: B) 1/8
questions.tip: For independent genes, break a dihybrid cross into separate monohybrid crosses and multiply the probabilities (product rule).

questions.text: A true-breeding tall pea plant is crossed with a true-breeding dwarf pea plant, and the F1 is self-pollinated to produce F2. What fraction of the tall F2 plants are expected to be true-breeding (homozygous) for tallness?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Determine the F2 genotypic ratio**
Selfing the F1 heterozygote (Tt x Tt) gives an F2 genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, as expected from the law of segregation.

**Step 2: Identify the tall plants among the F2**
Both TT and Tt show the tall phenotype since T is dominant, so tall plants make up 3 out of the 4 parts (TT + Tt = 1 + 2 = 3 parts), matching the 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

**Step 3: Identify which tall plants are true-breeding**
Only the TT genotype is true-breeding (homozygous) for tallness, since Tt plants will still segregate dwarf offspring on selfing; TT makes up 1 part out of the 3 parts of tall plants.

**Final Answer**
Out of the tall F2 plants (TT and Tt in a 1:2 ratio among themselves), only 1 in 3 is true-breeding TT.
Final answer: B) 1/3 of the tall F2 plants
questions.tip: Among F2 dominant-phenotype plants, the homozygous dominant to heterozygous ratio is always 1:2, so true-breeders are 1/3 of the dominant class.

questions.text: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, proposing that genes are located on chromosomes, was put forward by:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the historical context**
Mendel had proposed hereditary factors (genes) purely on the basis of breeding experiments, without knowing their physical location in the cell.

**Step 2: Identify the contribution of Sutton and Boveri**
Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri, working independently around 1902, noted that the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis paralleled the behaviour of Mendelian factors, and proposed that genes are carried on chromosomes.

**Step 3: Distinguish from Morgan's role**
Thomas Hunt Morgan later provided experimental proof of this theory using Drosophila and linkage studies, but the theory itself was first proposed by Sutton and Boveri.

**Final Answer**
The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance is credited to Sutton and Boveri, who connected chromosome behaviour with Mendelian genetics.
Final answer: B) Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri
questions.tip: Sutton-Boveri proposed the chromosomal theory; Morgan experimentally proved it using Drosophila.

questions.text: According to the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, Mendelian factors (genes) are located on:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the core proposal**
The chromosomal theory states that hereditary factors described by Mendel have a physical location within the cell.

**Step 2: Identify that location**
Sutton and Boveri observed that chromosomes, present in the nucleus, behave in a manner exactly parallel to the segregation and independent assortment of Mendelian factors, so they concluded genes reside on chromosomes.

**Step 3: Eliminate other cell structures**
Structures like the cell membrane, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus do not show behaviour matching the segregation of hereditary factors during gamete formation, so they were ruled out as the site of genes.

**Final Answer**
Genes are located on chromosomes present in the nucleus, and their transmission follows chromosome movement during meiosis.
Final answer: B) Chromosomes in the nucleus
questions.tip: Genes are arranged linearly on chromosomes; this is the physical basis of heredity.

questions.text: Which observation formed the strongest basis for the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance?
options: Dominant traits always mask recessive traits
The number of chromosomes is constant within a species
The behaviour of chromosome pairs during meiosis parallels the behaviour of gene pairs during inheritance
Chromosomes are visible only during cell division
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall Mendel's abstract postulates**
Mendel proposed that factors occur in pairs, that the two members of a pair separate during gamete formation, and that different pairs assort independently, all inferred purely from breeding ratios.

**Step 2: Compare with chromosome behaviour**
During meiosis, homologous chromosomes exist in pairs, separate from each other at anaphase I, and different homologous pairs orient and separate independently of one another.

**Step 3: Draw the parallel**
Sutton and Boveri noticed that this chromosomal behaviour matches, point for point, the segregation and independent assortment of Mendelian factors, providing a physical explanation for the previously abstract genetic laws.

**Final Answer**
The parallel behaviour of chromosomes and genes during meiosis was the key evidence linking heredity to chromosomes.
Final answer: C) The behaviour of chromosome pairs during meiosis parallels the behaviour of gene pairs during inheritance
questions.tip: Link segregation of alleles to anaphase I separation of homologous chromosomes - this parallel is the crux of the chromosomal theory.

questions.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan provided experimental support for the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance by studying:
options: Garden pea seed shape and colour
The white-eye mutation and its inheritance pattern in Drosophila melanogaster
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall Morgan's model organism**
Morgan worked with Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) because of its short life cycle, large progeny number, and easily observable variations, including a white-eyed mutant that arose among normally red-eyed flies.

**Step 2: Trace the inheritance pattern**
When Morgan crossed white-eyed males with red-eyed females, he found that the white-eye trait was transmitted in a pattern that correlated exactly with the transmission of the X chromosome, unlike Mendelian autosomal traits.

**Step 3: Connect gene to chromosome**
This correlation allowed Morgan to conclude that the gene for eye colour is located on the X chromosome, giving direct experimental proof that specific genes reside on specific chromosomes.

**Final Answer**
Morgan's Drosophila white-eye experiments provided the first solid experimental evidence linking a specific gene to a specific chromosome, validating the chromosomal theory.
Final answer: B) The white-eye mutation and its inheritance pattern in Drosophila melanogaster
questions.tip: Morgan's white-eyed Drosophila experiment is the classic proof-of-concept for both the chromosomal theory and sex-linked inheritance.

questions.text: A student observes that in a diploid organism, one member of each homologous chromosome pair moves to opposite poles during a particular meiotic stage, mirroring how the two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes. This event occurs during:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify what separates at each stage**
In mitosis, sister chromatids of each chromosome separate at anaphase, so the chromosome number and homologue pairing are not relevant there. In meiosis, two divisions occur, each with its own anaphase.

**Step 2: Distinguish anaphase I from anaphase II**
At anaphase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes (each still consisting of two sister chromatids) separate from each other and move to opposite poles, whereas at anaphase II, sister chromatids of each chromosome separate, similar to mitosis.

**Step 3: Relate to allele segregation**
Since the two alleles of a gene are carried on the two homologous chromosomes, their physical separation, matching the law of segregation, occurs specifically when homologues separate, i.e., at anaphase I.

**Final Answer**
The segregation of alleles corresponds to the separation of homologous chromosomes at anaphase I of meiosis, the cytological basis of Mendel's law of segregation.
Final answer: B) Anaphase I of meiosis
questions.tip: Anaphase I = homologues separate (basis of segregation); Anaphase II = sister chromatids separate (like mitosis).

questions.text: In the flowering plant Mirabilis jalapa, a cross between a red-flowered (RR) plant and a white-flowered (rr) plant produces F1 plants that are pink. This is an example of:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare F1 phenotype with parents**
Neither parental phenotype (red or white) appears in the F1; instead, an intermediate pink colour is seen, which is different from simple Mendelian dominance where F1 resembles one parent exactly.

**Step 2: Define incomplete dominance**
Incomplete dominance occurs when neither allele is completely dominant over the other, so the heterozygote shows a blended or intermediate phenotype between the two homozygous parents.

**Step 3: Rule out codominance and multiple allelism**
Codominance would show both parental phenotypes simultaneously and distinctly (not blended), and multiple allelism refers to a gene having more than two allelic forms in a population, neither of which matches the blended pink phenotype seen here.

**Final Answer**
The intermediate pink colour in Mirabilis jalapa F1 hybrids is the classic textbook example of incomplete dominance.
Final answer: B) Incomplete dominance
questions.tip: Mirabilis jalapa (4 o'clock plant) and snapdragon are the standard NCERT examples of incomplete dominance.

questions.text: In the AB blood group phenotype, both the A and B antigens are expressed simultaneously on the red blood cell surface. This phenomenon is called:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Examine what is expressed**
An individual with AB blood group shows both A antigen and B antigen fully and distinctly on the red blood cell surface, rather than a blended or intermediate antigen.

**Step 2: Define codominance**
Codominance occurs when both alleles of a gene are fully expressed in the heterozygote, with neither masking the other, so both phenotypes appear side by side.

**Step 3: Contrast with incomplete dominance**
In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows a single blended phenotype (like pink flowers), whereas in codominance both original phenotypes are separately and fully visible, matching what is seen in the IAIB genotype.

**Final Answer**
Since both A and B antigens are independently and fully expressed, the IA and IB alleles show codominance.
Final answer: B) Codominance
questions.tip: Incomplete dominance = blended phenotype; Codominance = both phenotypes expressed separately and fully (e.g., AB blood group, roan cattle).

questions.text: The ABO blood group system in humans is controlled by a single gene (I) that has how many allelic forms?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the concept of multiple alleles**
While a normal diploid individual carries only two alleles of a gene, a gene can exist in more than two allelic forms within a population, a phenomenon called multiple allelism.

**Step 2: Identify the ABO alleles**
The ABO blood group gene (I) exists in three allelic forms in the human population: IA, IB, and i (also written IO).

**Step 3: Note their relationships**
IA and IB are both dominant over i and codominant with each other, and any individual carries only two of these three alleles, but the population as a whole maintains all three.

**Final Answer**
The ABO blood group gene is a classic example of multiple allelism, existing as three alleles, IA, IB, and i, in the population.
Final answer: C) Three
questions.tip: Multiple alleles exist at the population level; an individual still carries only two of them. ABO blood group is the textbook example.

questions.text: In Mirabilis jalapa, when a pink-flowered plant (Rr) is crossed with another pink-flowered plant (Rr), what is the expected phenotypic ratio in the offspring?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the genotype-phenotype relationship**
In incomplete dominance, each genotype produces a distinct phenotype: RR gives red, Rr gives pink, and rr gives white, since heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype rather than resembling either homozygote.

**Step 2: Set up the cross**
Crossing Rr x Rr, each parent produces R and r gametes in equal frequency, giving a genotypic ratio of 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr in the offspring, exactly as in a standard monohybrid cross.

**Step 3: Convert genotype to phenotype directly**
Because there is no dominance to mask any genotype, the phenotypic ratio exactly mirrors the genotypic ratio: 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (Rr) : 1 white (rr).

**Final Answer**
Unlike complete dominance where phenotypic and genotypic ratios differ (3:1 versus 1:2:1), incomplete dominance gives identical phenotypic and genotypic ratios of 1:2:1.
Final answer: B) 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
questions.tip: In incomplete dominance, phenotypic ratio equals genotypic ratio (1:2:1) because every genotype has a unique phenotype.

questions.text: A child has blood group AB. Which of the following genotype combinations of the parents could explain this, assuming standard Mendelian inheritance of the ABO gene?
options: Both parents are group O (ii x ii)
One parent is group A (IAIA) and the other is group O (ii)
One parent is group A (IAi) and the other is group B (IBi)
Both parents are group AB (IAIB x IAIB) only
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the requirement for AB genotype**
A child with AB blood group must have the genotype IAIB, meaning it must receive one IA allele from one parent and one IB allele from the other parent.

**Step 2: Check each option for the presence of both alleles**
Two group O parents (ii x ii) can only pass i alleles, so they cannot produce an IAIB child; a group A (IAIA) x group O (ii) cross can give only IAi (group A) offspring, never IB.

**Step 3: Verify the correct option**
A group A parent with genotype IAi can pass either IA or i, and a group B parent with genotype IBi can pass either IB or i; therefore one possible combination is the IA gamete from the first parent fertilising with the IB gamete from the second parent, giving an IAIB (AB) child.

**Final Answer**
An IAi (group A) parent crossed with an IBi (group B) parent can produce an AB child, since each parent can contribute the allele the child needs.
Final answer: C) One parent is group A (IAi) and the other is group B (IBi)
questions.tip: For ABO blood group problems, always write out possible parental genotypes (homozygous or heterozygous) before assigning gametes.

questions.text: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder in which a single mutant gene causes mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation, and other symptoms simultaneously. This phenomenon, where one gene influences multiple, apparently unrelated phenotypic traits, is called:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the pattern of gene action**
Here, a single defective gene (which fails to properly break down the amino acid phenylalanine) is responsible for producing several distinct symptoms at once, rather than one gene affecting only one trait.

**Step 2: Define pleiotropy**
Pleiotropy is the phenomenon where a single gene influences multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits, often because the gene's product is involved in a metabolic pathway that has several downstream effects.

**Step 3: Eliminate the other terms**
Codominance and incomplete dominance describe how two alleles of one gene interact to determine one trait, and epistasis describes one gene masking the expression of another gene; none of these describe a single gene affecting many traits.

**Final Answer**
Because the single PKU gene mutation produces multiple simultaneous effects on the body, this is a case of pleiotropy.
Final answer: C) Pleiotropy
questions.tip: Pleiotropy: ONE gene, MANY traits. NCERT example: phenylketonuria.

questions.text: In Antirrhinum (snapdragon), which also shows incomplete dominance for flower colour, a cross between two pink-flowered (Rr) plants is expected to yield a red-flowered offspring in what proportion?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the incomplete dominance genotype-phenotype rule**
As in Mirabilis jalapa, RR gives red, Rr gives pink, and rr gives white in snapdragon, since the heterozygote is phenotypically intermediate.

**Step 2: Set up the Rr x Rr cross**
Selfing two pink (Rr) plants gives a genotypic ratio of 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr among the four equally likely offspring classes.

**Step 3: Identify the red-flowered class**
Only the RR genotype, which makes up 1 out of the 4 total parts, gives the red phenotype.

**Final Answer**
Since RR offspring make up 1/4 of the total, the proportion of red-flowered offspring from a pink x pink cross is 1/4.
Final answer: A) 1/4
questions.tip: Snapdragon and Mirabilis jalapa follow identical 1:2:1 incomplete dominance logic - practice the Punnett square for both.

questions.text: A man with blood group A (genotype IAi) marries a woman with blood group B (genotype IBi). What is the probability that their child will have blood group O?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: List gametes from each parent**
The IAi father produces IA and i gametes in equal proportion, and the IBi mother produces IB and i gametes in equal proportion.

**Step 2: Build the Punnett square**
Combining these gametes gives four equally likely genotypes: IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), and ii (O), each with a probability of 1/4.

**Step 3: Identify the genotype for group O**
Blood group O results only from the homozygous recessive genotype ii, since the i allele produces neither A nor B antigen and is recessive to both IA and IB.

**Final Answer**
Out of the four equally likely offspring genotypes, exactly one (ii) gives blood group O, so the probability is 1/4.
Final answer: B) 1/4
questions.tip: Group O requires ii; since i is recessive to both IA and IB, both parents must be heterozygous carriers of i for an O child to be possible.

questions.text: A geneticist is trying to determine whether the coat colour gene in a cattle breed shows incomplete dominance or codominance. Which observation in the heterozygote would specifically indicate codominance rather than incomplete dominance?
options: The heterozygote shows a uniform colour exactly intermediate between the two parental colours, such as pink from red and white
The heterozygote shows patches of both parental colours distinctly side by side, such as roan coat with distinct red and white hairs
The heterozygote shows only the colour of one parent completely
The heterozygote fails to show any colour at all
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Define the two phenomena precisely**
Incomplete dominance produces a single, uniform, blended phenotype in the heterozygote (a true intermediate, like pink), whereas codominance produces both parental phenotypes independently and distinctly, without blending.

**Step 2: Apply to cattle coat colour**
A roan coat consisting of a mixture of distinct red hairs and distinct white hairs side by side (not a blended pink hair colour) means both alleles are being separately and fully expressed in different hair follicles or regions.

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
A uniform intermediate colour describes incomplete dominance, showing only one parental colour describes complete dominance, and showing no colour would not represent either phenomenon.

**Final Answer**
Distinct patches of both parental colours appearing side by side, rather than a blended intermediate shade, is the hallmark of codominance, as seen in roan cattle coats.
Final answer: B) The heterozygote shows patches of both parental colours distinctly side by side, such as roan coat with distinct red and white hairs
questions.tip: Roan cattle and AB blood group are true codominance (both alleles fully expressed); a blended shade is incomplete dominance.

questions.text: In humans, sex determination follows the XX-XY system. Which parent determines the sex of the offspring?
options: The mother, since she is heterogametic
The father, since he is heterogametic and produces two types of gametes
Both parents equally contribute to determining sex
Neither parent; sex is determined randomly after fertilisation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the sex chromosome constitution of each parent**
In humans, females are XX (homogametic, producing only X-bearing eggs) and males are XY (heterogametic, producing two types of sperm, X-bearing and Y-bearing, in equal numbers).

**Step 2: Trace fertilisation outcomes**
Since the egg always carries an X chromosome, the sex chromosome contributed by the sperm determines the offspring's sex: an X-bearing sperm fertilising the egg gives XX (female), while a Y-bearing sperm gives XY (male).

**Step 3: Conclude which parent is decisive**
Because the mother always contributes an X, it is the father's sperm type that decides whether the zygote becomes male or female.

**Final Answer**
Since the father is heterogametic (XY) and produces both X- and Y-bearing sperm, he determines the sex of the child.
Final answer: B) The father, since he is heterogametic and produces two types of gametes
questions.tip: Heterogametic sex produces two types of gametes and thus determines offspring sex; in mammals this is the male (XY).

questions.text: In birds and butterflies, sex is determined by the ZW-ZZ system. Which sex is heterogametic in this system?
options: Neither sex; sex is determined by temperature
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the ZW system chromosome constitution**
In birds, males carry two similar sex chromosomes, ZZ, while females carry two different sex chromosomes, ZW.

**Step 2: Define heterogamety**
The heterogametic sex is the one that produces two different types of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes; since females are ZW, they produce Z-bearing and W-bearing eggs in equal numbers.

**Step 3: Contrast with males**
Males, being ZZ, produce only Z-bearing sperm, making them the homogametic sex in this system, the reverse of the mammalian XY system.

**Final Answer**
In the ZW-ZZ system found in birds, the female (ZW) is heterogametic and thus determines the sex of the offspring.
Final answer: B) Female (ZW)
questions.tip: ZW system (birds, some fish/reptiles) reverses the mammalian pattern - females are heterogametic (ZW), males are homogametic (ZZ).

questions.text: In grasshoppers, sex determination follows the XX-XO system. What is the chromosome constitution of the male grasshopper, and how many types of sperm does he produce?
options: XO; two types of sperm (X-bearing and without any sex chromosome)
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the XO system**
In the XX-XO system, females have two X chromosomes (XX), but males have only a single X chromosome and no corresponding second sex chromosome, written as XO.

**Step 2: Determine gamete types in the male**
During meiosis, the single X chromosome in the male goes to only one of the two poles, so half the sperm receive an X chromosome and the other half receive no sex chromosome at all.

**Step 3: Predict offspring sex**
An egg (always carrying one X) fertilised by an X-bearing sperm produces an XX (female) zygote, while fertilisation by a sperm with no sex chromosome produces an XO (male) zygote.

**Final Answer**
The male grasshopper is XO and produces two types of sperm, one with an X chromosome and one without any sex chromosome, determining the sex of the offspring.
Final answer: B) XO; two types of sperm (X-bearing and without any sex chromosome)
questions.tip: XO system: males have one fewer chromosome than females; sperm are either X-bearing or lack a sex chromosome entirely.

questions.text: In honeybees, sex determination occurs through haplodiploidy. Which statement correctly describes this mechanism?
options: Fertilised eggs develop into haploid males, unfertilised eggs into diploid females
Fertilised eggs (diploid) develop into females, and unfertilised eggs (haploid) develop into males
Both males and females develop from fertilised diploid eggs
Sex is determined by a pair of Z and W chromosomes as in birds
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the honeybee reproductive pattern**
In honeybees, the queen can lay both fertilised and unfertilised eggs, and the fate of the egg depends on whether fertilisation occurred, not on distinct sex chromosomes.

**Step 2: Trace the fertilised egg pathway**
A fertilised egg contains chromosomes from both the queen and a drone (father), making it diploid, and diploid individuals develop into females, either workers or a new queen.

**Step 3: Trace the unfertilised egg pathway**
An unfertilised egg contains only the chromosome set contributed by the queen through an unreduced egg, making it haploid, and haploid individuals develop into males (drones) through parthenogenesis.

**Final Answer**
This system, called haplodiploidy, means diploid fertilised eggs become females and haploid unfertilised eggs become males, with no separate sex chromosomes involved.
Final answer: B) Fertilised eggs (diploid) develop into females, and unfertilised eggs (haploid) develop into males
questions.tip: Haplodiploidy has no sex chromosomes at all - ploidy level itself (diploid vs haploid) decides sex; drones (males) are haploid.

questions.text: A couple has three daughters and is expecting a fourth child. Based on the principles of human sex determination, what is the probability that the fourth child will be a son?
options: Less than 1/2, since three daughters were already born
Exactly 1/2, since each fertilisation event is an independent trial with equal X- and Y-bearing sperm
More than 1/2, since a son is due after three daughters
Cannot be determined without knowing the mother's genotype
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the basis of sex determination in each pregnancy**
Each child's sex depends on whether the fertilising sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome, and a male produces X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm in equal (1:1) numbers.

**Step 2: Recognise independence of events**
Each fertilisation event is an independent random trial; the sex chromosome carried by the sperm that fertilises one egg has no influence on which type of sperm fertilises the egg in a subsequent, separate pregnancy.

**Step 3: Apply this to the given scenario**
Having had three daughters does not change the probability for the next child, since there is no memory or compensation mechanism in independent probabilistic events.

**Final Answer**
The probability of the fourth child being a son remains exactly 1/2, unaffected by the sex of the previous children.
Final answer: B) Exactly 1/2, since each fertilisation event is an independent trial with equal X- and Y-bearing sperm
questions.tip: Classic probability misconception (gambler's fallacy) - each birth is an independent event with 1:1 odds, regardless of prior births.

questions.text: The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome in humans, plays which critical role in sex determination?
options: It suppresses the development of male reproductive organs
It encodes the testis-determining factor that triggers development of the undifferentiated gonad into testes
It is responsible for producing estrogen in the ovary
It determines eye colour independent of sex
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the state of the embryonic gonad**
Early in human development, the gonad is undifferentiated and has the potential to develop into either testes or ovaries, depending on genetic signals it receives.

**Step 2: Identify the role of SRY**
The SRY (Sex-determining Region of Y) gene, present on the Y chromosome, encodes a protein called the testis-determining factor (TDF), which triggers the undifferentiated gonad to develop into testes.

**Step 3: Trace the consequence for the rest of development**
Once testes form, they secrete testosterone and other hormones that direct the development of male reproductive structures; in the absence of SRY (as in XX individuals), the gonad instead develops into ovaries.

**Final Answer**
The SRY gene on the Y chromosome is the key genetic switch that initiates testes development, making it central to the chromosomal determination of male sex in humans.
Final answer: B) It encodes the testis-determining factor that triggers development of the undifferentiated gonad into testes
questions.tip: SRY = testis-determining factor gene on Y chromosome; its presence/absence, not just chromosome count, is the molecular switch for testes vs ovary development.

questions.text: Linkage refers to the phenomenon in which:
options: Two genes located on different chromosomes are always inherited together
Two or more genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together
A single gene controls two unrelated traits
Two alleles of a gene are expressed simultaneously in the heterozygote
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the physical basis**
Genes located on the same chromosome are physically connected to one another as part of a single DNA molecule, unlike genes on different chromosomes which assort independently.

**Step 2: Define linkage**
Because genes on the same chromosome travel together into the same gamete during meiosis (unless separated by crossing over), they tend to be inherited together rather than assorting independently, a phenomenon called linkage.

**Step 3: Eliminate the distractors**
Genes on different chromosomes show independent assortment, not linkage; a single gene affecting multiple traits is pleiotropy; and simultaneous expression of both alleles in a heterozygote is codominance, none of which describe linkage.

**Final Answer**
Linkage specifically describes genes on the same chromosome being inherited together more often than expected by independent assortment.
Final answer: B) Two or more genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together
questions.tip: Linkage is the major deviation that limits Mendel's law of independent assortment for genes on the same chromosome.

questions.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan's dihybrid crosses in Drosophila using body colour and wing size genes showed a much higher frequency of parental-type offspring than the 9:3:3:1 ratio predicted by independent assortment. This result was explained by:
options: The two genes being located on the same chromosome and hence linked
The two genes being sex-linked recessive traits
A high mutation rate in Drosophila
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall Morgan's expectation and observation**
Based on independent assortment, a dihybrid cross should give offspring where parental combinations and recombinant combinations appear close to expected Mendelian proportions, but Morgan observed that parental-type combinations vastly outnumbered new (recombinant) combinations.

**Step 2: Interpret the deviation**
Such a deviation occurs when the genes being studied are not on separate chromosomes but are instead located on the same chromosome, so they tend to travel together into the same gamete rather than assorting independently.

**Step 3: Connect to the concept of linkage**
Morgan concluded that genes for body colour and wing size in Drosophila are physically linked on the same chromosome, explaining why parental combinations predominated over recombinant ones.

**Final Answer**
The excess of parental-type offspring over recombinants indicated that the two genes are linked on the same chromosome, a major experimental deviation from independent assortment.
Final answer: B) The two genes being located on the same chromosome and hence linked
questions.tip: Excess parental-type offspring compared to recombinant types in a dihybrid cross is the classic signature of linkage.

questions.text: Recombination frequency between two linked genes is primarily used to:
options: Determine the dominant allele between the two genes
Estimate the relative distance between the two genes on the chromosome
Determine whether the genes are autosomal or sex-linked
Calculate the total number of chromosomes in the organism
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how recombinants are formed**
Recombinant gametes arise from crossing over between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, which exchanges segments of DNA between linked genes.

**Step 2: Relate crossover frequency to physical distance**
Genes that are located farther apart on a chromosome have a higher chance of a crossover occurring between them, producing more recombinant gametes, whereas genes very close together are rarely separated by crossing over.

**Step 3: Apply this relationship**
By measuring the percentage of recombinant offspring in a test cross (the recombination frequency), geneticists can estimate the relative distance between two linked genes, since recombination frequency is roughly proportional to the physical distance between them.

**Final Answer**
Recombination frequency serves as a measure of the relative distance between linked genes on a chromosome, forming the basis of genetic mapping.
Final answer: B) Estimate the relative distance between the two genes on the chromosome
questions.tip: Higher recombination frequency = genes farther apart (weaker linkage); lower recombination frequency = genes closer together (tighter linkage).

questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes complete linkage from incomplete linkage?
options: In complete linkage, genes are on different chromosomes; in incomplete linkage, they are on the same chromosome
In complete linkage, linked genes are always inherited together with no recombinants produced; in incomplete linkage, some recombinant gametes are produced due to occasional crossing over
Complete linkage occurs only in plants, while incomplete linkage occurs only in animals
Complete linkage always produces a 9:3:3:1 ratio, while incomplete linkage produces a 1:1 ratio
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Define complete linkage**
In complete linkage, two genes are located so close together on the same chromosome that crossing over between them essentially never occurs, so they are always transmitted together as parental combinations, with no recombinant offspring produced.

**Step 2: Define incomplete linkage**
In incomplete linkage, the genes are still on the same chromosome but far enough apart that crossing over occurs occasionally, producing a small proportion of recombinant gametes in addition to a majority of parental-type gametes.

**Step 3: Eliminate incorrect statements**
Both phenomena involve genes on the same chromosome (ruling out the first option), linkage type is not tied to plants versus animals, and neither always gives the ratios mentioned in the last option since actual ratios depend on the specific recombination frequency.

**Final Answer**
The key distinction is the presence or absence of recombinant offspring: complete linkage produces none, while incomplete linkage produces a smaller proportion of recombinants alongside a majority of parental types.
Final answer: B) In complete linkage, linked genes are always inherited together with no recombinants produced; in incomplete linkage, some recombinant gametes are produced due to occasional crossing over
questions.tip: True complete linkage is rare; most linked genes show incomplete linkage with some recombination due to crossing over.

questions.text: In a test cross involving two linked genes, out of 1000 offspring, 420 and 410 show the parental phenotypes while 90 and 80 show recombinant phenotypes. What is the recombination frequency between the two genes?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify total recombinant offspring**
Recombinant offspring are those with the two recombinant phenotypic classes, so add 90 and 80 to get a total of 170 recombinant offspring out of 1000.

**Step 2: Calculate recombination frequency as a percentage**
Recombination frequency is defined as the number of recombinant offspring divided by the total number of offspring, expressed as a percentage: 170 divided by 1000, multiplied by 100.

**Step 3: Verify using parental class as a check**
The parental classes (420 + 410 = 830) plus the recombinant classes (170) should sum to the total offspring (1000), confirming 830 + 170 = 1000, which checks out.

**Final Answer**
Dividing 170 recombinants by 1000 total offspring and multiplying by 100 gives a recombination frequency of 17%, indicating the two genes are linked but with moderate distance between them.
Final answer: B) 17%
questions.tip: Recombination frequency (%) = (recombinant offspring / total offspring) x 100; always add both recombinant classes together first.

questions.text: Three genes, P, Q, and R, are linked on the same chromosome. The recombination frequency between P and Q is 5%, between Q and R is 15%, and between P and R is 20%. Based on this data, what is the most likely gene order on the chromosome?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the mapping principle**
Recombination frequency is roughly proportional to the physical distance between two genes, so genes with a smaller recombination frequency are closer together, and genes with a larger recombination frequency are farther apart.

**Step 2: Identify the gene pair that is farthest apart**
The largest recombination frequency given is between P and R (20%), suggesting that P and R are the two genes at the outer ends of the map, with some other gene lying between them.

**Step 3: Place the middle gene**
Since P and Q have a small recombination frequency (5%) and Q and R have an intermediate recombination frequency (15%), and 5% plus 15% is approximately equal to the 20% distance between the outer genes P and R, gene Q must lie between P and R.

**Final Answer**
The additive relationship of the recombination frequencies (5% plus 15% is approximately 20%) places Q between P and R, giving the gene order P-Q-R.
Final answer: B) P-Q-R
questions.tip: Genetic map distances are roughly additive; the gene pair with the largest recombination frequency marks the two ends, and the third gene sits between them if its distances to each end sum close to that value.

questions.text: Haemophilia, a genetic disorder characterised by failure of blood clotting, is inherited as a(n):
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the location of the haemophilia gene**
The gene responsible for haemophilia is located on the X chromosome, not on any autosome, which is why the disorder shows a sex-linked pattern of inheritance rather than the simple autosomal patterns Mendel studied.

**Step 2: Recall its dominance relationship**
The haemophilia allele is recessive to the normal allele, meaning a female needs two copies of the defective allele (on both her X chromosomes) to be affected, while a male needs only one copy since he has only a single X chromosome.

**Step 3: Note the consequence of this pattern**
This explains why haemophilia is far more common in males than females, since males are hemizygous for X-linked genes and cannot be protected by a second, normal X chromosome as females can.

**Final Answer**
Haemophilia is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait, making males much more frequently affected than females.
Final answer: C) X-linked recessive trait
questions.tip: Haemophilia and colour blindness are the two classic NCERT examples of X-linked recessive disorders in humans.

questions.text: Red-green colour blindness is much more common in men than in women because the trait is:
options: Y-linked, so only sons can inherit it from their fathers
X-linked recessive, so a male needs only one copy of the allele to be affected
Autosomal dominant, requiring only one copy in either sex
Caused by an infection more common in men
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the chromosomal location of the gene**
The gene for red-green colour vision is located on the X chromosome, and the colour-blind allele is recessive to the normal allele.

**Step 2: Compare male and female genotypes**
A male has only one X chromosome (XY), so if that single X carries the recessive colour-blind allele, he is colour-blind since there is no second X to carry a normal, masking allele.

**Step 3: Contrast with females**
A female has two X chromosomes (XX) and therefore needs the recessive allele on both X chromosomes to be colour-blind; if she has even one normal allele, she is a carrier but not colour-blind herself, making the condition much rarer in females.

**Final Answer**
Because males are hemizygous for X-linked genes, a single recessive allele is enough to cause colour blindness in men, making it far more common in males than in females.
Final answer: B) X-linked recessive, so a male needs only one copy of the allele to be affected
questions.tip: Hemizygous males express any X-linked recessive allele they carry, since there is no second X allele to mask it.

questions.text: Criss-cross inheritance, first described by Morgan for the white-eye trait in Drosophila, refers to the pattern in which:
options: A trait is passed from father to son only
A trait is passed from mother to daughter only
A trait present in the father is passed to the daughters, who then pass it to their sons, without appearing in the sons of the original father
A trait appears equally in all offspring regardless of sex
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the original Drosophila cross**
Morgan crossed a white-eyed male fly with a red-eyed (normal) female; since the white-eye allele is X-linked recessive, the F1 females (who receive one X from each parent) become carriers, while F1 males (who receive their only X from the mother) are red-eyed.

**Step 2: Trace the F2 pattern**
When these carrier F1 females are crossed with normal males, the white-eye trait reappears in the F2 generation, but specifically in the sons, not in the daughters, showing that the trait effectively passed from the original father to his grandsons through his carrier daughters.

**Step 3: Define the term precisely**
This alternating, sex-linked transmission pattern, where a father's trait shows up in his daughters' sons rather than his own sons, is called criss-cross inheritance.

**Final Answer**
Criss-cross inheritance describes an X-linked trait passing from a father through his (carrier) daughters to his grandsons, rather than following simple parent-to-offspring transmission.
Final answer: C) A trait present in the father is passed to the daughters, who then pass it to their sons, without appearing in the sons of the original father
questions.tip: Criss-cross inheritance is the defining feature of X-linked recessive traits: father to daughter (carrier) to grandson.

questions.text: A carrier woman for haemophilia (XHXh) marries a normal man (XHY). What proportion of their sons is expected to be haemophilic?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: List the gametes from each parent**
The carrier mother (XHXh) produces XH and Xh eggs in equal proportion, while the normal father (XHY) produces XH and Y sperm in equal proportion.

**Step 2: Build the Punnett square**
Combining these gametes gives four equally likely offspring genotypes: XHXH (normal daughter), XHXh (carrier daughter), XHY (normal son), and XhY (haemophilic son).

**Step 3: Focus specifically on the sons**
Among the offspring, sons are either XHY (normal) or XhY (haemophilic), each with equal probability, since sons receive their single X chromosome only from the mother.

**Final Answer**
Of the sons produced, half are expected to be haemophilic (XhY) and half normal (XHY), so 50% of the sons are affected.
Final answer: C) 50% of the sons
questions.tip: For X-linked recessive traits, a carrier mother passes the allele to half her sons (who are then affected) and half her daughters (who become carriers).

questions.text: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous normal for colour vision. What is expected in their children regarding colour blindness?
options: All sons and daughters will be colour-blind
All daughters will be carriers, and all sons will have normal vision
All sons will be colour-blind, and all daughters will have normal vision
Half the sons and half the daughters will be colour-blind
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Assign genotypes to the parents**
The colour-blind father has genotype XcY, and the homozygous normal mother has genotype XCXC, where Xc is the recessive colour-blind allele and XC is the normal dominant allele.

**Step 2: Determine the gametes**
The father produces Xc and Y gametes, while the mother produces only XC gametes, since she is homozygous.

**Step 3: Combine gametes to find offspring genotypes**
Daughters receive the father's Xc and the mother's XC, giving genotype XCXc (carrier, phenotypically normal since XC is dominant); sons receive the father's Y and the mother's XC, giving genotype XCY (phenotypically normal).

**Final Answer**
Because the mother contributes only normal alleles, all daughters become unaffected carriers and all sons have completely normal vision, illustrating the criss-cross pattern of X-linked inheritance.
Final answer: B) All daughters will be carriers, and all sons will have normal vision
questions.tip: When the mother is homozygous normal, ALL daughters of an affected father become carriers, but sons cannot inherit the father's X-linked trait at all.

questions.text: A haemophilic man marries a carrier woman for haemophilia. What is the probability that their daughter will be haemophilic?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Assign genotypes**
The haemophilic father has genotype XhY, and the carrier mother has genotype XHXh, since haemophilia is X-linked recessive.

**Step 2: List gametes**
The father produces Xh and Y gametes, while the mother produces XH and Xh gametes in equal proportion.

**Step 3: Determine daughter genotypes specifically**
Daughters always receive the father's X chromosome, which is Xh, combined with either the mother's XH or Xh gamete, giving two possible daughter genotypes: XHXh (carrier, unaffected) or XhXh (haemophilic), each equally likely among daughters.

**Final Answer**
Half of the daughters are expected to be XhXh and therefore haemophilic, giving a 50% probability, a relatively rare situation only possible because the father himself is affected.
Final answer: C) 50%
questions.tip: A haemophilic daughter requires the recessive allele from BOTH parents - this needs an affected father AND at least a carrier mother.

questions.text: In a family pedigree, a trait appears in a grandfather, skips his daughter (who appears unaffected), and reappears in her son (the grandson), but never appears in any daughters of that generation. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Note the skipping pattern**
The trait skips a generation (the daughter is unaffected) but reappears in the next, suggesting the daughter is a heterozygous carrier rather than being affected herself, which is typical of a recessive condition.

**Step 2: Note the sex-specific reappearance**
The trait reappears only in a grandson, not in any granddaughters, indicating that the pattern is linked to the sex chromosomes rather than distributed equally among autosomal offspring.

**Step 3: Apply the criss-cross logic**
An X-linked recessive allele from the grandfather is passed to his daughter (who becomes an unaffected carrier since her other X is normal), and she then has a 50% chance of passing that same allele to her sons, who, being hemizygous, would express the trait; her daughters could only be carriers, not affected, unless the father also contributed the allele.

**Final Answer**
This skip-a-generation, male-only reappearance pattern is the classic signature of X-linked recessive inheritance, exactly matching Morgan's criss-cross inheritance pattern.
Final answer: C) X-linked recessive inheritance
questions.tip: Pedigree clue for X-linked recessive: affected males, carrier daughters, trait skips a generation and reappears in grandsons.

questions.text: Down syndrome in humans is caused by:
options: Deletion of a segment of chromosome 21
The presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21)
A single gene mutation on the X chromosome
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the normal chromosome number**
A normal human somatic cell contains 46 chromosomes, arranged as 23 homologous pairs, including two copies of chromosome 21.

**Step 2: Identify the abnormality in Down syndrome**
Down syndrome results from nondisjunction, an error during meiosis in one of the parents, leading to a gamete with an extra copy of chromosome 21; fertilisation with a normal gamete then produces a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two.

**Step 3: State the resulting karyotype**
This condition, called trisomy 21, gives an individual with 47 chromosomes in total instead of the normal 46, causing the characteristic physical and developmental features of Down syndrome.

**Final Answer**
Down syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 21, i.e., the presence of an extra (third) copy of chromosome 21, resulting in 47 total chromosomes.
Final answer: B) The presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21)
questions.tip: Down syndrome = trisomy 21 = 47 chromosomes total, caused by nondisjunction during gamete formation.

questions.text: A patient shows a karyotype of 45 chromosomes with a single X chromosome and no second sex chromosome (45,X0), along with short stature and rudimentary ovaries. This condition is known as:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Analyse the karyotype**
The karyotype 45,X0 shows a total of 45 chromosomes with only a single X chromosome and no Y or second X chromosome, indicating monosomy of a sex chromosome.

**Step 2: Match the karyotype to the syndrome**
This specific sex chromosome monosomy, where an individual has only one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome, is diagnostic of Turner syndrome, which affects phenotypic females.

**Step 3: Confirm with the clinical features**
Turner syndrome is characterised by a female phenotype with short stature, a webbed neck, and non-functional or rudimentary ovaries (ovarian dysgenesis) leading to sterility, matching the description given.

**Final Answer**
The 45,X0 karyotype with short stature and rudimentary ovaries is characteristic of Turner syndrome, a sex chromosome monosomy.
Final answer: B) Turner syndrome
questions.tip: Turner syndrome: 45,X0 (monosomy X), female phenotype, sterile due to rudimentary ovaries. Klinefelter is the opposite (extra X in males).

questions.text: A phenotypically male individual has a karyotype of 47,XXY, along with feminised body features, sparse facial hair, and enlarged breasts (gynaecomastia). This condition is known as:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Analyse the karyotype**
The karyotype 47,XXY shows one extra X chromosome in addition to a normal male XY complement, giving a total of 47 chromosomes, an example of sex chromosome trisomy.

**Step 2: Match to the syndrome**
This specific pattern of an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY) is the defining feature of Klinefelter syndrome, arising from nondisjunction of the X chromosome during gamete formation in either parent.

**Step 3: Confirm with clinical features**
Because the individual has a Y chromosome, the overall phenotype is male, but the extra X chromosome disrupts normal hormonal balance, producing feminised features such as gynaecomastia (breast development), sparse body hair, and sterility.

**Final Answer**
The 47,XXY karyotype with male phenotype but feminised features is characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome.
Final answer: C) Klinefelter syndrome
questions.tip: Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY, male with feminised features and sterility; caused by nondisjunction of sex chromosomes.

questions.text: Sickle cell anaemia results from a single amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain of haemoglobin. This substitution specifically is:
options: Valine replaced by glutamic acid at the sixth position
Glutamic acid replaced by valine at the sixth position
Glycine replaced by alanine at the first position
Leucine replaced by lysine at the third position
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the nature of the mutation**
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a point mutation (a single base substitution) in the gene coding for the beta-globin chain of haemoglobin, changing the sequence of just one codon.

**Step 2: Identify the specific amino acid change**
This mutation changes the codon at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain, causing the amino acid glutamic acid (which is normally present) to be replaced by valine.

**Step 3: Connect to the disease mechanism**
This substitution changes the surface property of the haemoglobin molecule, causing haemoglobin to polymerise into fibrous chains under low oxygen tension, which distorts red blood cells into a sickle shape and leads to the symptoms of the disease.

**Final Answer**
The defining molecular change in sickle cell anaemia is glutamic acid being replaced by valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain.
Final answer: B) Glutamic acid replaced by valine at the sixth position
questions.tip: Sickle cell anaemia: point mutation, glutamic acid to valine substitution at position 6 of beta-globin chain, autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder.

questions.text: Thalassemia is a genetic blood disorder that differs mechanistically from sickle cell anaemia in that thalassemia results from:
options: A single amino acid substitution in haemoglobin causing abnormal shape
Reduced or absent synthesis of one of the globin chains (alpha or beta) of haemoglobin due to mutations or deletions
An extra chromosome in the affected individual
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the nature of sickle cell anaemia for contrast**
Sickle cell anaemia involves a qualitative defect, a single amino acid substitution that alters the structure and behaviour of an otherwise normal quantity of haemoglobin.

**Step 2: Identify the nature of thalassemia**
Thalassemia, in contrast, is a quantitative disorder in which mutations, often deletions, in the genes controlling either the alpha-globin or beta-globin chains reduce or completely stop the synthesis of that particular globin chain.

**Step 3: Connect to clinical consequences**
The resulting imbalance between alpha and beta chain production leads to abnormal haemoglobin molecules, ineffective red blood cell production, and anaemia, with severity depending on how many of the relevant globin genes are affected.

**Final Answer**
Unlike sickle cell anaemia's structural defect, thalassemia arises from reduced or absent synthesis of a globin chain, making it a quantitative haemoglobin disorder inherited as an autosomal recessive Mendelian trait.
Final answer: B) Reduced or absent synthesis of one of the globin chains (alpha or beta) of haemoglobin due to mutations or deletions
questions.tip: Sickle cell anaemia = qualitative defect (wrong amino acid); Thalassemia = quantitative defect (too little or no globin chain made).

questions.text: Two individuals, both carriers for sickle cell trait (HbAHbS), have children. What proportion of their offspring is expected to suffer from full-blown sickle cell anaemia (HbSHbS)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Assign genotypes and gametes**
Both parents have the genotype HbAHbS, and since sickle cell anaemia follows simple Mendelian autosomal inheritance, each parent produces HbA and HbS gametes in equal proportion.

**Step 2: Build the Punnett square**
Combining these gametes from both parents gives four equally likely offspring genotypes: HbAHbA, HbAHbS, HbAHbS, and HbSHbS, following the standard monohybrid cross pattern.

**Step 3: Identify the affected genotype**
Only the homozygous HbSHbS genotype results in full-blown sickle cell anaemia, since the condition is recessive and a single normal HbA allele (as in the heterozygote) is sufficient to prevent full disease expression under normal oxygen conditions.

**Final Answer**
As in any standard monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, 1 out of 4 (25%) of the offspring are expected to be HbSHbS and therefore affected by full sickle cell anaemia.
Final answer: B) 25%
questions.tip: Sickle cell anaemia cross HbAHbS x HbAHbS follows the same 1:2:1 genotypic ratio as any monohybrid cross - 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% normal.

questions.text: Down syndrome is strongly correlated with increasing maternal age at the time of conception. What is the underlying cytological explanation for this correlation?
options: Older mothers have a higher rate of new point mutations in chromosome 21
Oocytes remain arrested in meiosis for many years, and the prolonged arrest increases the risk of nondisjunction of chromosome 21 during meiotic division
Older fathers produce sperm with more chromosome 21 copies
Down syndrome is caused by an infection that becomes more likely with maternal age
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall human oocyte development**
In human females, oocytes begin meiosis before birth but arrest in prophase I of meiosis I and remain suspended in this state for years to decades, resuming meiosis only just before ovulation.

**Step 2: Identify the cytological risk associated with prolonged arrest**
The longer an oocyte remains arrested, the more time there is for the meiotic spindle apparatus and the mechanisms holding homologous chromosomes together to deteriorate, increasing the chance that chromosome 21 fails to separate properly (nondisjunction) when meiosis finally resumes.

**Step 3: Connect nondisjunction to Down syndrome**
Nondisjunction of chromosome 21 during meiosis produces an egg with an extra copy of chromosome 21; if such an egg is fertilised, the resulting zygote has trisomy 21, causing Down syndrome.

**Final Answer**
The prolonged meiotic arrest of oocytes in older mothers increases the probability of chromosome 21 nondisjunction, explaining the well-documented correlation between advanced maternal age and Down syndrome incidence.
Final answer: B) Oocytes remain arrested in meiosis for many years, and the prolonged arrest increases the risk of nondisjunction of chromosome 21 during meiotic division
questions.tip: Maternal age effect in Down syndrome relates to prolonged oocyte arrest in meiosis I, increasing nondisjunction risk over time - this is a favourite NEET conceptual link.
